about: A clock repairer and his shop

lines.text: In a narrow shop below an old block of flats, Mr Tan repairs
clocks and watches. He learnt the trade from his father, which opened the
lines.note: 'Which' is for things. A person takes 'who'.

lines.text: shop more than fifty years ago. In those days, a clock were an
lines.note: Agreement: 'a clock' is one thing, so it is 'was'.

lines.text: expensive thing, and families would rather mend one than buying another. Mr Tan
lines.note: Verb form: 'would rather mend … than buy' — both verbs stay plain.

lines.text: still uses his father’s tools, which he keeps in a wooden drawer.
Each repair demands great patient, for some parts are smaller than a grain
lines.note: Word form: after 'great' a noun is needed — 'patience'.

lines.text: of rice. He often works for many hour under a bright lamp, and
he never hurries. Customers are fewer these days, since most people simply replace
a watch when it stopped working. Even so, a few regulars continue to
lines.note: Tense: this is what people do nowadays, so it is 'stops'.

lines.text: bring him clocks that have been in his families for generations. He treats
lines.note: Pronoun: the families belong to the regulars, so it is 'their'.

lines.text: each one in great care. Mr Tan knows that his shop may close
one day, but he intends to keep every clock ticking until then.
